newsitem.title: CROATIA: Britain's Cook says patience with Balkans runs out.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Cook says patience with Balkans runs out.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook on Wednesday outlined his government's tough new approach to the countries of former Yugoslavia, saying true peace must be achieved in the region before international patience wore thin.

"...The patience of the international community is running out on the slow progress in implementing the Dayton agreement (on Bosnia)," Cook told reporters after meeting Croatian President Franjo Tudjman and Foreign Minister Mate Granic.

He was referring to a peace treaty signed in Dayton, Ohio, in late 1995, which stopped the bloodshed in Bosnia. Progress in implementing the treaty, however, has been stalled by nationalist Croat, Serb and Moslem local leaders.
In his first tour of the region, Cook has been taking a tough line with Bosnia's Moslem and Serb leaders, demanding more a consistent implementation of the peace accords.

"I have assured Tudjman now that there is a very firm common goal from the whole international community, particularly Germany, United States and Britain that we want to see the Dayton agreement through," Cook said.
"That's why we've set the deadlines by which steps must be taken and by which they must be implemented by local leadership," he told reporters.

The steps include allowing all refugees to return to the homes they fled during the 3-1/2 years of war and handing over indicted war criminals to an International War Crimes Tribunal (ICTY) in the Hague.
Of more than 70 people indicted by the ICTY, only a handful are in its custody and two have been sentenced so far.

Croatia has handed over one Bosnian Croat suspect and another surrendered himself. But Zagreb has taken no action to apprehend others, claiming they were in the Bosnian Croat territory, out of reach of Croatian police.
Cook said he sought help with Tudjman and Granic "to make sure that those who have been charged, should they enter Croatia or should they be in the Croat part of Bosnia, are handed over for trial".
Countering criticism that indictees have had to wait for months before trials began, Cook said Britain was now single-handedly paying for a second courtroom in The Hague.
"There is now no reasonable excuse for war criminals not to be handed over. If they are innocent, they have nothing to fear."
Cook said Britain "very much wants to see Croatia entering modern Europe and a family of European nations".

"But it can only do so if it embraces standards of a modern European state", he said, pointing out the issues of free media and minority rights, which forced the Council of Europe in 1995 to postpone Zagreb's membership bid.

In remarks on Tudjman's refusal to even consider joining any new Balkans association, such as the U.S.-backed SECI (South European Cooperation Initiative) aimed at promoting loose borders and free trade in the region, Cook said:

"I want to assure the people of Croatia that there is no plot, no conspiracy by the international community to create a south-eastern political union. Former Yugoslavia is finished, nobody is attempting to rebuild it."
